name: Basil
description: Basil is a tender herb from the mint family, best known for its sweet, peppery aroma in pesto, tomato salads, Thai curries, and fresh herb sauces. Oregano, mint, tarragon, or holy basil can stand in depending on whether the dish needs Mediterranean sweetness or sharper anise notes.
culinaryContext: Fresh basil varieties are used as aromatic leafy herbs in Mediterranean and Southeast Asian cooking.
howToUse: Add fresh leaves near the end of cooking for aroma, or bruise them into sauces, salads, curries, and herb pastes. Use dried basil earlier in simmered dishes.
sourceName: Wikipedia / Wikidata culinary herb and spice references

sourceSummary: Basil, also called great basil, is a culinary herb of the family Lamiaceae (mints). It is a tender plant and is used in cuisines worldwide. In Western cuisine, the generic term "basil" refers to the variety also known as Genovese basil or sweet basil. Basil is native to tropical regions from Central Africa to Southeast Asia. In temperate climates basil is treated as an annual plant, but it can be grown as a short-lived perennial or biennial in warmer horticultural zones with tropical or Mediterranean climates.

sourceSummary: Black pepper is a flowering vine in the family Piperaceae, cultivated for its fruit, which is usually dried and used as a spice and seasoning. The fruit is a drupe (stonefruit) which is about 5 mm in diameter, dark red, and contains a stone which encloses a single pepper seed. Peppercorns and the ground pepper derived from them may be described simply as pepper, or more precisely as black pepper, green pepper, or white pepper.

sourceSummary: Cardamom, sometimes cardamon or cardamum, is a spice made from the seeds of several plants in the genera Elettaria and Amomum in the family Zingiberaceae. name: Tarragon
description: Tarragon has a distinctive anise-like flavor that defines béarnaise sauce, chicken, fish, eggs, vinegar, and French herb blends. French tarragon is more refined than Russian types. Use it fresh when possible and avoid long cooking; chervil, fennel fronds, or basil can substitute lightly.
culinaryContext: Used across fresh and dried herb traditions in home and restaurant cooking.
howToUse: Use the leaf in small measured amounts, then adjust after tasting. It works especially well with chicken, egg, mustard. Add it near the end for fresher aroma, or earlier when you want a softer background note.
sourceName: Wikipedia / Wikidata culinary herb and spice references

name: Tasmanian pepper
description: Tasmanian pepper is an Australian native pepper berry with sharp heat, fruity notes, and a distinctive herbal edge. It suits meats, mushrooms, sauces, and native-inspired blends. Mountain pepper is a close substitute; black pepper can add bite but not the same regional aroma.
culinaryContext: Used where its fruity, peppery, pungent character (moderate warmth) defines the dish, rather than as a generic pepper substitute.
howToUse: Use it deliberately with game, berries, roasted vegetables. It brings fruity, peppery, pungent notes with moderate warmth, so start small and adjust to taste.
sourceName: Wikipedia / Wikidata culinary herb and spice references

name: Thai basil
description: Thai basil has sturdier leaves and a clear anise-clove note that holds up better in hot dishes than sweet basil. It is common in Thai curries, Vietnamese noodle bowls, stir-fries, and herb platters. Add it near the end for perfume, or use holy basil, sweet basil, mint, or cilantro when matching Southeast Asian flavors.
culinaryContext: Fresh basil varieties are used as aromatic leafy herbs in Mediterranean and Southeast Asian cooking.
howToUse: Add fresh leaves near the end of cooking for aroma, or bruise them into sauces, salads, curries, and herb pastes. Use dried basil earlier in simmered dishes.
sourceName: Wikipedia / Wikidata culinary herb and spice references
howMuchToUse: Use a handful of leaves in curries, stir-fries, noodle bowls, and soups. Add just before serving to preserve its anise-like aroma.

name: Thyme
description: Thyme brings earthy mint and gentle floral warmth to soups, stews, roast chicken, mushrooms, beans, and herb blends. It holds up well under heat, so it can simmer longer than basil or parsley. Oregano, rosemary, marjoram, or savory can substitute in small amounts.
culinaryContext: Used across fresh and dried herb traditions in home and restaurant cooking.
howToUse: Use the leaf in small measured amounts, then adjust after tasting. It works especially well with rosemary, garlic, lemon. Add it near the end for fresher aroma, or earlier when you want a softer background note.
sourceName: Wikipedia / Wikidata culinary herb and spice references
howMuchToUse: Use a few sprigs or 1/2 teaspoon dried thyme in soups, stews, roasted vegetables, and poultry. It handles longer cooking well.

name: Torch ginger
description: Torch ginger is a spice used for its spicy, warm, citrusy character. Cooks most often match the root or rhizome with coconut milk, lime, fish, chili, where it adds a distinct seasoning note instead of a generic background flavor. It brings noticeable heat, so add it gradually and balance with salt, fat, or acidity. If a recipe needs a substitute, consider ginger, galangal, turmeric and adjust the quantity to match the dish.
culinaryContext: Commonly used in Indonesia cooking contexts.
howToUse: Use the root or rhizome in small measured amounts, then adjust after tasting. It works especially well with garlic, soy sauce, lemon. It can be bloomed briefly in oil or added during cooking for gentle warmth.

name: Turmeric
description: Turmeric is the golden rhizome of Curcuma longa, used fresh or dried for earthy bitterness, color, and gentle warmth. It anchors curry powders, dals, rice dishes, soups, pickles, and golden milk. Bloom the powder in fat or simmer the fresh root; combine with black pepper, ginger, cumin, or coconut for balance.
culinaryContext: Used across global spice traditions, both alone and in blended seasonings.
howToUse: Use the root or rhizome in small measured amounts, then adjust after tasting. It works especially well with black pepper, ginger, coconut. It can be bloomed briefly in oil or added during cooking for gentle warmth.
sourceName: Wikipedia / Wikidata culinary herb and spice references
howMuchToUse: Use 1/4 to 1 teaspoon ground turmeric in curries, rice, soups, or marinades; combine with fat and pepper for fuller flavor.

name: Wasabi
description: Wasabi is a pungent Japanese rhizome known for sharp vapor-like heat that rises through the nose and fades quickly. It is served with sushi, sashimi, noodles, and dressings. Fresh wasabi is delicate and rare; horseradish-based pastes are stronger and less nuanced.
